title: GPU SKU matching & cost heuristics — lab notes and proposal
content:
Purpose and audience:
This doc captures lab findings, deployment-level heuristics, and an actionable autoscaling + SKU recommendation for customer POCs that need predictable latency under cost constraints. Primary audience: solutions engineering, platform eng, and the customer technical leads during the POC.

High-level problem statement:
Customers frequently come with mixed traffic patterns: steady background inference for user-facing features plus spiky batch/ingestion jobs. They want committed Dedicated capacity that minimizes overpay while meeting 99th percentile latency SLOs. Our job is to: 1) pick an optimal mix of SKUs, 2) size baseline and burst capacity, and 3) prescribe autoscaling rules and pre-warm heuristics that minimize cold-start tokens and guards against SLA breaches.

Workload profile used in lab:
- Token profile: median request = 60 tokens, p95 = 420 tokens, heavy tail up to 2k tokens for long-form generation.
- QPS patterns: baseline steady 35 rps, daily peak 550 rps (short spikes, 3–12 minutes), scheduled nightly batch runs (~4k concurrent mini-requests across several jobs for 25 minutes).
- Model family: Llama-family 2.0-style encoder-decoder variants; we tested two quantization profiles (int8 and 4-bit NNC-optimized).

SKU candidates evaluated (lab nomenclature):
- SKU-A: H100-80GB (nvlink, best FP16 latency)
- SKU-B: A100-80GB (widely available, good throughput)
- SKU-C: L4-48GB (cost-optimized, smaller KV cache)

Empirical observations (short):
- SKU-A yields ~22–28% lower p95 latency on long sequences vs SKU-B at same concurrency, but per-hour cost is ~1.6x SKU-B in our spot-equivalent pricing.
- SKU-C is cost effective for short/median sequences but saturates earlier due to smaller password/kv region — tail latency jumps at p95 when long requests appear.
- Mixed-pool (SKU-C baseline + SKU-A burst) gives best cost vs p95 coverage for mixed workloads tested.

Sizing heuristic (the lane model):
We propose a two-lane pool model:
- Baseline lane: persistent, cheaper SKUs to cover steady-state and common tail (median→p90). Purpose: reduce committed spend and provide stable cache locality.
- Burst lane: fewer, high-SLA SKUs that accelerate long sequences and absorb short spikes. Purpose: preserve p95/p99 and avoid widespread queueing.

Sizing steps (operational recipe):
1) Translate customer target SLO into latency budget (e.g., 95th <= 350ms for 60-token median).
2) Run 15-min synthetic replay with customer token distribution to estimate token-per-second consumption and effective throughput per SKU under target quantization.
3) Compute baseline capacity = ceil((steady_qps * avg_tokens_per_request) / tokens_per_sec_per_SKU_baseline) + 10% safety buffer.
4) Compute burst buffer = ceil((peak_qps - steady_qps) * avg_tokens_per_request / tokens_per_sec_per_SKU_burst). Keep burst lane at least 1 node minimum for hot-standby.
5) Add warm pool size = round( baseline_capacity * 0.15 ) or min(2 nodes) — this is a pre-warmed subset kept cold-start-free.

Example numbers (from lab replay):
- steady_qps = 35 rps, avg_tokens = 60 → token rate = 2100 tps.
- SKU-C tokens/sec (measured, int8) = ~650 tps per card. Baseline_capacity_C = ceil(2100/650)=4 cards → add 10% → 5 cards. Warm pool = 1 card.
- peak_qps = 550 rps → peak_tokens = 33k tps. SKU-A tokens/sec (measured, fp16) = ~4500 tps per card. Burst_needed_A = ceil((33k-2100)/4500)=7 cards.

Cost estimates (lab rate assumptions; replace with customer pricing):
- SKU-A: $9.00/hr (on-demand equivalent for lab)
- SKU-B: $5.45/hr
- SKU-C: $1.90/hr
Running scenario monthly: 30 days, baseline persistent: 5 * SKU-C = 5 * $1.90 * 24 * 30 = $6,840/month.
Burst monthly (assume average burst utilization 15% of the month in short bursts): 7 * SKU-A * 0.15 * 24 * 30 = 7 * $9.00 * 0.15 * 720 = $6,804/month.
Total monthly (~lab sim): ~$13.6k/month (baseline + burst). Note: actual committed pricing and reservations reduce both components — include negotiation line-item.

Autoscale policy proposal (practical rules):
- Signals: combined queue depth + token-rate predictor + CPU/GPU utilization. Avoid scaling on short single-sample latencies.
- Scale-up triggers: if moving-average token-rate (60s) exceeds 85% of provisioned token throughput for 2 consecutive 30s windows → add 1 burst node. For sustained growth (10m) allow incremental additions up to configured burst ceiling.
- Scale-down triggers: if token-rate stays below 60% of provisioned capacity for 5 minutes and queue depth < 2 → remove 1 node. Use exponential cool-down (min 10m) to avoid thrash.
- Pre-warm policy: detect scheduled job windows (from customer cron or observed recurring patterns). For predicted >30% step-up in token-rate within 10m, pre-warm warm-pool nodes. Pre-warm nodes are charged as reserved but marked as ready; they are not in baseline until needed.
- Graceful degradation: when total capacity saturation >95% and no burst nodes available, fallback to lower-capacity model variant (quantized) but keep prompt truncation and quality-preserving rate-limiter. Documented trade-off table required in customer runbook.

Operational runbook (short):
- Onboard steps: run 2-hour replay, produce steady/peak table, pick lane mix, run 24-hour stress sim.
- Day-of-POC checklist: verify pre-warm jobs, enable metric hooks (per-route token-rate, queue-depth), create emergency increase policy (manual escalation to +25% capacity).
- Escalation: if p95 latency > configured SLO for >10 minutes despite scaling to burst ceiling → notify solutions-eng + platform on-call and enable immediate fallback model with a single toggle in the console.

Risk and open questions:
- Spot/Preemptible vs on-demand mix: lab used conservative on-demand equivalents. If customer relies on spot, factor 20–30% availability delta and plan a higher burst buffer.
- Model variant compatibility: not all model variants maintain identical output characteristics when quantized — tie regression tests to the rollout.
- Cost transparency: make per-route token-level cost visible in the POC dashboard so customers can see where long-tail requests drive spend.

Recommendations for the sales/technical narrative:
- Offer a baseline commitment (3–6 month) sized for p90 plus a burst pool sized for the measured p95.
- Emphasize warm-pool as the primary lever for reducing cold-starts vs simply buying more baseline cards.
- Present two bundled options: Cost-first (baseline heavy, cheaper SKUs, larger warm pool) and SLA-first (smaller baseline, more burst A100/H100 capacity).

Next actions and ownership:
- Action: run 24h replay with customer-provided traces (owner: Maya Chen) — due in 4 business days.
- Action: produce a formal cost sheet using actual cloud quotes and present in next customer workshop (owner: Jonah Rivera) — due in 7 business days.
- Action: add a minimal test in onboarding flow that validates warm-pool scaling behavior (owner: Evan Schultz) — due in 3 sprints.

Appendix — quick checklist for engineering handoff:
- Provide tokens-per-second per-SKU CSV from lab run.
- Attach the replay harness script and parameter set used. (See linked github PR.)
- Include one-line summary of expected monthly cost under baseline assumptions.

Notes to self / rough thoughts (informal):
- Consider an adaptive warm-pool that grows with 7-day moving average of daily peak width rather than a static percentage. Might reduce cost in patterns that have shorter spikes.
- Investigate multi-tenant packing heuristics for SKU-A to reduce the burst node count when many small requests arrive; effective if KV cache sharing can be preserved.
- Worth adding a small experiment to measure p99 delta between 8-bit and int8 model paths on H100.

End of doc.
